description:
Space tech developer and multi-time NASA Space Apps winner (global nominee, local awards, honorable mention). My goal is building another high-impact, award-winning project under experienced leadership. Join to turn ideas into global reality!
Looking for: Teammates skilled in software development, UI/UX, data analysis, hardware, or presentation design.
summary:
Lunar Outpost is a 3D educational STEM game prototype in which children aged 7–12 manage a four-person base at the Moon’s south pole. Players monitor power, life support, food production, and communications. When the cooling line starts leaking, they can follow the orange pipe and close the valve, carry a spare part to repair the line, or buy time with the backup pump. The backup pump drains the battery; shutting down the greenhouse reduces the heat load but delays the harvest.
We developed the project to bring core science, technology, engineering, and mathematics [STEM] concepts to life, enabling children to see through their own decisions how operating one system affects another during a space mission. Our goal was to help them understand cause and effect, practice engineering trade-offs, and develop systematic thinking skills in the process. We built the game terrain using elevation and imagery data collected from lunar orbit. We designed the cooling scenario around a documented leak on a Soyuz spacecraft docked to the International Space Station.
Lunar Outpost occupies a unique place in the literature by transforming a specific case study—grounded directly in the actual cooling leak incident on a Soyuz spacecraft docked to the International Space Station and NASA's lunar south pole orbital data, rather than generic and fictional space scenarios—into a hands-on STEM simulation that children aged 7–12 can experience through physical interaction.
details:
Detailed Project Description Core Gameplay Loop Players inspect the lunar base systems on site. When a fault occurs, they respond, track the effects of their decision using the game indicators, and finish the shift with a mission report.

1. Start your shift Use the checklist to track your checks of the research center, greenhouse, power system, and antenna.

2. Respond to the leak
Close the valve, fit the spare connector, and restore the flow.

3. Prioritize based on available power The backup pump drains the battery. Shutting down the greenhouse reduces the heat load but delays the harvest.

4. Review the mission results
The report confirms that the supplies were delivered, Earth acknowledged receipt, and all four crew members reached the shelter.

What exactly does it do? 

Lunar Outpost shows children aged 7–12 how the systems of a space base depend on one another and teaches them about technical processes used in real space missions. Players inspect the research center, greenhouse, antenna, and power system on site. They then respond to a cooling failure, carry the harvest back to the base, call the crew to the shelter during a radiation drill, and transmit a science report to Earth. Through these activities, children learn firsthand how to manage a four-person base at the Moon’s south pole and how closely power, life support, food production, and communications are connected. 

How does it work? 

Players start their first shift with a task checklist. As they walk to the equipment and interact with it, completed checks are marked on the list. When the cooling line starts leaking, on-screen markers show the locations of the valve and the spare part. Players can follow the orange pipe to close the valve and carry the spare part to attempt a repair of the main line, or isolate the line and use the backup pump. The base terrain is based on real elevation and location data from lunar orbit. When the base is in shadow, battery power is limited, so it matters which devices stay on. Players can use the game indicators to track how their decisions affect power, temperature, and the harvest. 

What benefits does it aim to provide? 

Through this gameplay experience, we aim to help children understand cause and effect, develop systems thinking skills, and learn the following specific concepts: 

Interactions Between Systems and Trade-off Analysis: Understand how switching one system on or off affects other systems [for example, running the backup pump drains the battery, while shutting down the greenhouse reduces the heat load but delays the harvest]. 

Real Space Missions and Crisis Management: Learn how to identify a fault, isolate a line using a valve, and carry out a repair through a scenario inspired by a real leak documented on a Soyuz spacecraft docked to the International Space Station. 

Lunar Geography and Management of Limited Resources: Learn to prioritize limited energy based on periods of shadow in a south pole setting built using real elevation and imagery data from lunar orbit. 

Crew Safety and Life Support: Understand why human life and essential life support take priority by directing the four-person crew to the shelter during a radiation hazard. 

Players can address the same problem in two different ways and compare the outcomes. For example, in one run they may keep the backup pump on and use more power; in another, they may shut down the greenhouse temporarily and delay the harvest. The discussion then moves from “Which button should I press?” to “Why should I keep this system running under these conditions?” 

What do we hope to achieve? Our goal is for players to explain, in their own words, the decision they made by the end of a mission, the scientific and technical reasoning behind it, and what it cost. The project is currently a playable prototype. We used automated gameplay checks to test the game rules. As a next step, we propose an age-appropriate pilot study using pre-tests and post-tests to compare how children justify similar power and cooling decisions before and after the mission.

What are the benefits for players? 

By directly experiencing how subsystems depend on one another and how resources must be traded off, children move from carrying out procedural actions [“Which button should I press?”] to explaining the causes and strategy behind their choices [“Why should I keep this system running with these constraints?”]. 

They learn about the connection between real NASA data and its applications in space in a fun and engaging way. 

They experience how the systems of a space base are connected and the kinds of decisions astronauts make. 

Our goal is to use NASA’s orbital data for the lunar south pole and scenarios based on real failures in space [the Soyuz leak] to help children aged 7–12 experience the cause-and-effect relationships among power, life support, food, and communications systems, and develop systems thinking through an accessible simulation that requires no special hardware. The main limitations at this stage are that the project is still a single-player prototype for 64-bit Windows; thermodynamic and astrophysical processes have been reduced to simplified mechanics suitable for the age group; terrain data covers only the area around the base; and the effect of the intended educational outcomes on children has not yet been measured in field tests [pre-test/post-test]. 

Design and Creativity Process: Human Vision Uniting Science with Play 

The design process of Lunar Outpost began with a single fundamental question: How can we make a 7 to 12-year-old child feel the complex system balances faced by a real aerospace engineer, without boring formulas, using only a sense of wonder and discovery? The answer we gave to this question shaped the entire creative backbone of the project. Although technical tools and artificial intelligence assistants increased our coding speed, the soul, pedagogical fiction, and atmosphere of the game were entirely designed with the human intuition of our team. 

From Data to Emotion: Atmosphere and Space Design 

We did not want to leave NASA's Moon south pole [Shackleton Crater] data merely as cold numerical maps. We transformed the data into a living world where a child can walk inside, feel the chill of the shadow, and appreciate the value of energy. Instead of the player solving a crisis by clicking through a menu screen, we envisioned that they should notice the malfunction themselves, reach the valve by following the orange cooling pipe with their eyes, and physically carry the spare part. This "hands-on experience" approach was consciously chosen to give the child the feeling of being the true person in charge of the base, rather than a passive observer.

Pedagogy of Crisis: "Reasoned Decision" Instead of "Right Answer" Unlike traditional educational games, in Lunar Outpost we did not force the player into a single correct answer. While drawing inspiration from the real Soyuz leak on the International Space Station, we left gray areas for the children: Should they turn on the backup pump and consume energy, or stop the greenhouse and delay the harvest? We transformed this dilemma into a safe playground where children can experiment without the fear of making mistakes. Our creativity focused on translating complex thermodynamics and resource management rules [trade-offs] into visual indicators and concrete outcomes that the 7 to 12 age group can grasp intuitively. The Crew's Story and Empathy We designed the base not just as a facility consisting of machines, but as the home of a four-person human crew. The mechanics of calling the crew to the shelter when a radiation alarm goes off were added to instill a sense of human responsibility beyond technical data. Through this, children realize that managing systems actually means protecting human life. In summary; the Godot Engine and artificial intelligence tools provided the bricks that allowed us to build this world, but what turned those bricks into a meaningful story and learning journey that will leave a mark in a child's imagination was our team's creative perspective. What tools did we use? We developed the game using Godot Engine and GDScript. We imported samples of elevation and imagery data collected from lunar orbit into the game in JSON format. To speed up development and improve technical efficiency, we used OpenAI Codex as a strategic assistant for writing and debugging code. We carried out development and technical checks on a computer and prepared the playable release for 64-bit Windows. The game is played using a keyboard and mouse and requires no special hardware. To let the judges review the project without installing it, we made a video showing the playable prototype’s user experience [UX] and core mechanics available through the YouTube link on page 2 of the demo slides. Alignment with STEM Disciplines Lunar Outpost allows children [aged 7–12] to experience space exploration not merely as an adventure, but as a tangible engineering problem within an interactive laboratory environment. Our project’s direct connection to the STEM disciplines is outlined below: [S] Science: Players experience the harsh environmental conditions of the Moon’s south pole [permanently shadowed regions, extreme cold, radiation hazards, and their effects on solar panels]. Fundamental scientific concepts—such as operating a greenhouse system, plant growth cycles, and coolant thermodynamics—are integrated directly into the gamemechanics. 

[T] Technology: The project is a digital simulation developed using Godot Engine and GDScript. Real elevation maps [DEM] and mosaics acquired from NASA’s orbital instruments [LRO LOLA, LROC, and ShadowCam] were imported into the digital environment, while AI tools [OpenAI Codex] were utilized as a strategic technological assistant to optimize the development process. 

[E] Engineering: Systems engineering and trade-off analysis, which form the core of the project, require children to make sound engineering decisions during a failure [such as the scenario inspired by the Soyuz coolant leak]. Players engage in hands-on engineering practice by managing energy, operating the backup pump, isolating valves, and establishing the link between life support and power systems. 

[M] Mathematics: Players must manage a limited battery capacity and power budget. Energy consumption, harvest delay times, charging rates, and the coordinate/elevation data of the lunar surface [structured as an 81×81 grid at 5-meter intervals] reinforce mathematical proportional reasoning and resource planning skills. 

6. Use of Artificial Intelligence 

 

The core concept, scientific data integration, game mechanics, and user experience [UX] design of Lunar Outpost were shaped entirely by our team’s creative vision and engineering decisions. We used AI tools as strategic assistants to speed up development and improve technical efficiency. 

Within the architecture designed by our team, we used OpenAI Codex to help write code, debug it, and create automated gameplay tests. We also used ChatGPT to help structure and edit the language of the project documentation and submission materials. 

All in-game images in the presentation were captured directly from the working prototype developed by our team. The Shackleton Crater mosaic, which forms part of the game’s scientific foundation, was incorporated directly from official NASA archives. In the interest of transparency, the project documentation clearly states the scope of all AI-assisted code and text contributions.
dataRefs: We used a grid of 81 × 81 elevation samples at 5-meter intervals from the Site04 map to build approximately 400 × 400 meters of in-game terrain. The elevations and slopes players walk on are based on these data. The base buildings and adjustments to the ground around the facilities are part of the game design.
We aligned the relevant portion of this image, collected from lunar orbit, with the elevation map. We used the image for the surface tones and the LOLA data to shape the terrain.
We added the mosaic, created with contributions from NASA, KARI, and ASU, to the in-game science card. Players can compare the crater’s sunlit rim with its permanently shadowed interior.

We used the Soyuz coolant leak documented in the report as the starting point for the crisis scenario. The repair steps, temperature values, and mission durations in the game were simplified for educational purposes.
We used this open map product as the base image for Earth in the game’s sky.
Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI): Images from ShadowCam, carried aboard KARI’s Danuri spacecraft, contribute to the mosaic used in the Shackleton science card.
